summary:
Article 24 of the Constitution of the Republic of Kosovo prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, and the 2015 Law on Protection from Discrimination extends that protection to gender identity. Outright International's March 2026 overview records that implementation of both provisions remains inconsistent in practice, so the guarantees a visitor can cite are stronger than what is reliably delivered.

Legal gender recognition runs through the courts rather than an administrative procedure. In January 2019 Blert Morina's application for a name and gender-marker change on Kosovo identity documents was before the Constitutional Court of Kosovo, and applicants in Kosovo followed closely the European Court of Human Rights ruling in X v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, which held that a surgical requirement for changing a gender marker violates private-life rights.

Partner recognition remains unadopted law. Parliament rejected a law recognising same-sex civil unions in March 2022. Prime Minister Albin Kurti pledged in April 2024 to legalise same-sex civil unions, and a Justice Ministry working group was drafting the relevant bill, but as of February 2026 Parliament had still not adopted the new Civil Code amid fierce opposition that included the ruling party. IntelliNews reports that the draft Civil Code's gender-neutral marriage language would open the way to same-sex marriage if it enters into force.

Public LGBTI organising is visible in Prishtina, where the third annual Pride Parade was held alongside a week of exhibitions, conferences and discussions organised by the Center for Equality and Liberty. The CSGD annual report for 2022 documented intolerance and hatred, with hate speech by politicians common during the Civil Code debates, and an artist received death threats over a painting.
tangentialFactors:
A Reuters report of May 2024 framed the debate as Muslim-majority Kosovo considering same-sex unions amid fierce opposition, indicating the political climate a visitor would encounter rather than any rule applying to them.

ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 records that parliament had already voted against amendments recognising same-sex couples in 2022, and that during Pride week Prime Minister Kurti said he would do his utmost to secure adoption of the Civil Code. The same review notes that Kosovo Pride Week was held under the motto 'I love you as you are!', a public signal of organising capacity that coexists with the hostility recorded in the CSGD report.
localsOnly:
The constitutional and statutory protections, and their inconsistent enforcement, apply to Kosovo residents on the same terms as to visitors, and residents carry the burden of the court-supervised gender-recognition route described above.

Residents are the parties directly affected by the stalled Civil Code: its adoption or rejection determines whether same-sex couples obtain recognition of civil unions or marriage under Kosovo family law, and the outcome remained unresolved as of February 2026.

Organisations including the Center for Equality and Liberty and CSGD provide the domestic infrastructure for reporting intolerance and hate speech, which the 2022 CSGD report found to be common among politicians during legislative debates.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses entry, visa or border screening of trans visitors, including whether identity documents are inspected for gender markers on arrival; that question is unresolved here.

The outcome of Blert Morina's Constitutional Court case on name and gender-marker change is not sourced beyond its pending status in January 2019, and no source states the current evidentiary or medical requirements for legal gender recognition in Kosovo.

The inventory does not cover access to gender-appropriate facilities, healthcare or hormone treatment for visitors, nor the penalties attaching to hate crimes or the enforcement record of discrimination complaints brought under the 2015 law.
